title: The 24% APR Card
prompt: You get approved for your first credit card: $1,500 limit, 24.99% APR. The app suggests you "just pay the minimum, $35, to stay in good standing."
method_guidance: This is a credit card — a line of credit from the bank that lets you borrow now and repay later, with interest if you carry a balance.
Every purchase is money the bank fronts you; you owe it back, plus interest on whatever isn't paid off by the due date.
Applying and using the card means agreeing to the APR, the minimum payment terms, and any fees in the cardholder agreement.
Paying only the minimum lets interest compound on the rest — a $1,500 balance at 24.99% can take years and cost hundreds extra if you only pay the minimum.
Pull up the card's full terms (APR, grace period, fees) and run the numbers on paying in full each month versus minimum-only before you swipe.

title: Your Paycheck After Taxes
prompt: Your first full-time offer is $50,000/year — about $4,167/month. Your first pay stub shows $3,190 deposited, after federal, state, Social Security, Medicare, and a 401(k) contribution.
method_guidance: This is your real take-home pay — the amount left after mandatory taxes and any benefits you opted into.
The gross $4,167 came from your employer; the roughly $977 difference is split between government withholding and your own retirement savings.
Accepting the job and benefits enrollment means agreeing to these withholdings automatically each pay period.
Budgeting off the $4,167 instead of $3,190 leads to a shortfall every single month — the deposited number is the only one that matters for spending.
Read your full pay stub line by line and match each deduction against your benefits enrollment paperwork.

title: The 'Guaranteed 30% Return' DM
prompt: A polished account with client testimonials messages you: "Our AI trading algorithm guarantees 30% monthly returns. Minimum investment $500, act before spots fill."
method_guidance: This is almost certainly an investment scam, dressed up with the language of AI and algorithmic trading to sound credible.
The $500 would come from you, sent to an account or wallet the scammer controls — not into any real regulated investment.
Sending the money means agreeing to trust a stranger's unverifiable claim, with no contract, regulator, or recourse behind it.
The most likely outcome is losing the full amount, sometimes after being shown fake "returns" to convince you to send more.
No legitimate investment can guarantee returns — verify any offer through a licensed platform or regulator (like checking FINRA/SEC registration) before sending anything.

title: Buy Now, Pay Later for Rent?
prompt: You're short this month. A new app offers to pay your $1,200 rent for you today, and you repay it in four installments over six weeks, plus a $40 service fee.
method_guidance: This is a short-term loan marketed as a rent-payment service — you're borrowing against your next paychecks.
The app fronts your landlord the money now; the repayments come out of your bank account on their schedule, not yours.
Signing up means agreeing to four future automatic withdrawals plus the fee, on top of whatever you owe next month anyway.
If next month's rent is due before you've caught up, this can start a cycle where you're always borrowing against income you haven't earned yet.
Compare the $40 fee against a payment plan directly with your landlord, or a lower-cost overdraft/credit option, before signing up.

title: The Robo-Advisor Auto-Invest
prompt: An investing app offers to auto-invest $200 every payday into an AI-optimized portfolio, no confirmation needed once you turn it on.
method_guidance: This is automated investing — an algorithm buying assets on your behalf according to a strategy you selected once.
The $200 comes from your bank account on a recurring schedule, same as any other automatic transfer.
Turning it on means agreeing to let the algorithm rebalance and invest without asking you each time, within whatever settings you chose.
Automatic investing can build savings consistently, but markets can also drop — recurring investing doesn't remove investment risk.
Check the app's fee structure, what it's actually invested in, and whether it's a registered, regulated advisor before connecting your bank account.

title: Your Roommate's Payment Request
prompt: Your roommate sends a $340 request for "utilities" through a P2P payment app. You don't have an itemized bill to check it against.
method_guidance: This is a peer-to-peer payment request — money moving directly between two personal bank accounts, with no bank or company double-checking the amount.
The money would come straight from your checking account into your roommate's, once you approve.
Approving the request means agreeing the amount is correct — P2P apps generally don't offer dispute protection like a credit card would.
If the amount is wrong, getting money back depends entirely on your roommate, not the app — there's usually no chargeback.
Ask for the actual utility bill or a breakdown before paying, and keep a receipt/screenshot of what you agreed to and why.

title: The Stablecoin Payroll Offer
prompt: A freelance client offers to pay your $3,000 invoice in a USD-pegged stablecoin instead of a bank transfer, saying "it's basically the same as dollars, but faster."
method_guidance: This is a stablecoin — a cryptocurrency designed to track the value of a real currency like the US dollar, but issued and backed outside the traditional banking system.
The $3,000 in value comes from your client, converted into the stablecoin instead of moved through your bank.
Accepting it means agreeing to hold and eventually convert an asset that isn't legal tender and isn't FDIC-insured the way bank deposits are.

"Basically the same as dollars" depends entirely on the issuer keeping full backing — most major stablecoins have held their peg, but some have broken it before, and conversion to cash can involve fees or delays.
Look up the specific stablecoin's issuer, reserves, and track record, and check what it actually costs and how long it takes to convert to real dollars in your bank.

title: The AI Agent Auto-Renewed Your Insurance
prompt: You gave a budgeting AI assistant permission to "optimize and manage" your subscriptions and policies. It just renewed your car insurance at a higher rate without asking, saying it was "the best available option at renewal time."
method_guidance: This is an AI agent acting with standing authority — it made a real financial decision on your behalf, not just a recommendation.
The higher premium is now committed to come out of your account on the policy's normal billing schedule.
When you granted "manage" permission, you agreed to let it act without asking each time — the renewal was inside the authority you gave it.
Unless you catch it and switch, you'll keep paying the higher rate every renewal period going forward.
Review exactly what authority you granted (in the app's permissions settings), and check the new policy's actual terms against competitors before letting it stand.

title: The Student Loan Interest Statement
prompt: Your annual loan statement shows: principal balance $22,000, but you paid $2,400 this year and the balance only dropped by $600.
method_guidance: This is a loan statement showing how your payments split between interest (the cost of borrowing) and principal (what you actually still owe).
Most of your $2,400 in payments went to interest that accrued on the balance, not toward reducing what you originally borrowed.
Taking out the loan meant agreeing to an interest rate that keeps charging on the unpaid balance until it's fully paid off.
At this pace, paying off the loan will take far longer and cost far more in total interest than the original amount borrowed.
Use the loan servicer's amortization breakdown (or a calculator) to see the interest-vs-principal split, and check if extra payments toward principal are allowed without penalty.

title: The NFT Concert Ticket
prompt: A concert sells tickets as NFTs on a blockchain marketplace for $150 — the seller says it's "more secure than a normal ticket and you can resell it for a profit."
method_guidance: This is a blockchain-based ticket — ownership recorded on a public ledger instead of (or alongside) a traditional ticketing system.
The $150 goes to the seller or marketplace, and in return you receive a token that's supposed to represent your entry to the event.
Buying it means agreeing to the marketplace's and venue's specific rules for how that token gets checked at the door.

If the venue doesn't actually honor the token, the marketplace shuts down, or the resale market never materializes, you could be left with no entry and no value — "can resell for profit" is never guaranteed.
Confirm directly with the venue's official site that this specific token is a recognized, honored ticket before paying, not just the seller's word.
